messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh, a 61-year-old South Asian man, had been married for over three decades and worked at a non-profit organization focused on community support. His life took an unexpected turn when he was involved in a life-threatening motor vehicle collision several months ago. The event left Rajesh with vivid recollections that continue to haunt him, profoundly impacting his daily functioning. The trauma began as Rajesh was driving home late one evening. As he navigated through the dimly lit streets, another car swerved into his lane without warning. The sound of metal on metal reverberated as they collided, sending both vehicles spinning out of control. In that moment, the texture of the steering wheel under his hands and the sight of shattered glass and twisted metal imprinted themselves onto Rajesh’s memory with an almost photographic clarity. Since then, Rajesh has become acutely sensitive to certain triggers that remind him of the crash. The tactile sensation of a specific rough material, like the steering wheel, immediately transports him back to the horror of that night. When he encounters this texture in his daily life, such as while handling materials at work or even when touching the car door handle, it evokes vivid flashbacks and the intense fear that defined the accident. These triggers not only bring back the memory but also heighten Rajesh’s sense of threat. Unexpected movements nearby cause him to react as if danger is imminent, and loud sounds from traffic or his environment startle him deeply. The sudden return of the crash imagery makes it seem like he is reliving the event in real-time, with all its terror and unpredictability. These flashbacks are accompanied by visual memories that feel so intense they almost overwhelm him. Rajesh’s heightened sense of threat further exacerbates his experience of memory recall. His fear intensifies as he anticipates the return of these terrifying images, which can be triggered at any moment by a sound or movement. He constantly worries about being caught off guard and reliving the trauma, causing him to avoid places that remind him of the crash. In his role as a non-profit worker, Rajesh has found himself avoiding certain materials and textures associated with the steering wheel of his car. This avoidance has impacted his ability to engage fully in his work responsibilities, sometimes leading to delays or mistakes. His wife also notices changes in his behavior, as he becomes easily startled by sounds or movements that others might not notice. What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was an incident at work where a colleague inadvertently triggered one of his flashbacks during a conversation about safety measures for community programs. This experience left him feeling overwhelmed and exposed, making it clear that he needed professional support. His greatest fear is losing control in public or becoming too incapacitated by these memories to function effectively. Rajesh hopes that therapy will help him manage the intense triggers and reduce his sense of threat so that he can regain a sense of normalcy in both his personal life and his work environment. He wants to be able to drive again without being overwhelmed by fear, to engage fully with his colleagues, and to live each day without constantly reliving the traumatic event.
